In brief

The narrator of Cyclops reports John Wyse Nolan as "saying it was Bloom gave the ideas for Sinn Fein to Griffith to put in his paper all kinds of jerrymandering, packed juries and swindling the taxes off of the Government and appointing consuls all over the world to walk about selling Irish industries." His suspicion that Bloom would engage in shady schemes seems unremarkable enough in this chapter of antisemitic canards, but the idea that Bloom masterminded the Irish separatist organization known as Sinn Féin is outlandish in completely different ways. Not only is Bloom fictional and Arthur Griffith quite real, but Bloom is never seen engaging in political activity in the novel and Griffith was notoriously antisemitic, so the thought of these two putting their heads together sounds absurd. But Joyce probably knew of politcally active Jews who advised Griffith, and also of one who brought Hungarian revolutionary ideas to Ireland—a key part of the mix of assertions in Cyclops. 

At more length

Griffith founded Sinn Féin (Irish for "We Ourselves") in 1905 as a political party focused on achieving independence from Great Britain. In an article published in the United Irishman in 1900, and in a series of further articles beginning in January 1904, Griffith called for unification of various Irish nationalist groups, withdrawal of MPs from the British parliament to found a separate Irish parliament, cultivation of economic self-reliance, and nonviolent resistance to coercive British laws. He took hope from Hungary, where an independence movement began with a violent revolution against Viennese control in 1848, produced a very short-lived republic in 1849, persisted through years of tense negotiations, and ended in the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867. This Ausgleich established a "dual monarchy" in which Austria and Hungary were parts of a single empire but governed by separate parliaments.

In response to Irish demands for Home Rule, and inspired by this continental model, William Ewart Gladstone and the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) proposed in the 1870s that Britain and Ireland should form a dual monarchy, but nothing came of it. Griffith attempted to revive the idea in his 1904 newspaper articles, and in a book later that year titled The Resurrection of Hungary: A Parallel for Ireland. The two situations had significant differences, one being that Hungary contained its own suppressed and disenfranchised populations of non-Hungarian peoples. In Stephen Hero, which Joyce wrote in 1904 and 1905, Stephen criticizes the analogy as being "built haphazard upon very inexact knowledge": Irish nationalists see Hungary as an example of "a long-suffering minority, entitled by every right of race and justice to a separate freedom, finally emancipating itself," but they ignore "aggressions of the Magyars upon the Latin and Slav and Teutonic populations, greater than themselves in number" (62). Despite this difference, events would confirm Griffth's perception of a strong "parallel."

As in Hungary, armed revolt came first, in the form of the unsuccessful Easter Rising of 1916. Griffith opposed violent action, and his Sinn Féin party did not join the conflict. Two years later, though, it won a crushing majority in the general election of December 1918. In 1919, following Griffith's plan, the party's MPs refused to take up their seats in Westminster and instead proclaimed themselves the first parliament of the Irish Republic. Negotiations with the British followed, and in 1921 a treaty delegation led by Griffith agreed to the formation of the Free State—like Hungary a separate nation, but still part of the British Empire. The Irish civil war of 1922-23 resulted from continuing bitter disagreement between those who, like Griffith and Michael Collins, thought half a loaf better than none and those who, like Éamon de Valera, felt that the parliamentary compromise betrayed the republican cause.

Since Joyce made his protagonist the son of a Hungarian immigrant, he might well have been tempted to connect Bloom to Griffith's Hungarian proposal. And indeed people in the chapter where Sinn Féin "ideas" are mentioned do make much of Bloom's Hungarian connection. The narrator says that he is guilty of "Selling bazaar tickets or what do you call it royal Hungarian privileged lottery. True as you're there. O, commend me to an israelite! Royal and privileged Hungarian robbery." The charge of criminality refers to the relatively minor transgression of selling tickets to a foreign lottery, which British law forbade. In Lestrygonians Bloom thinks of "that lodge meeting on about those lottery tickets," and the Cyclops narrator thinks, "He was bloody safe he wasn't run in himself under the act that time as a rogue and vagabond only he had a friend in court." Apparently Bloom protested ignorance of the law to his friends in the Masonic lodge, and one of them convinced a judge to let him off. 

But rumors of a more substantial conspiracy are swirling around in the scuttlebutt of the bar. When Ned Lambert asks, "Is he a jew or a gentile or a holy Roman or a swaddler or what the hell is he?," Martin Cunningham replies that Bloom is "a perverted jew" from "a place in Hungary and it was he drew up all the plans according to the Hungarian system. We know that in the castle." Saying that Bloom "drew up all the plans" does not sound like a description of a man peddling lottery tickets. It does fit with the notion that Bloom was advocating a program of anti-imperial resistance. There can be little doubt that government officials "in the castle" would want to keep their eyes on something like that, no matter how peaceful the plan.

The narrator responds at least to the minor Hungarian scheme, and perhaps to both of them, as evidence that Bloom is engaged in countless nefarious activities: "all kinds of jerrymandering, packed juries and swindling the taxes off of the Government and appointing consuls all over the world to walk about selling Irish industries." Except possibly for the charge of cheating the government of taxes, these are fantastical libels. No one else in the bar says anything of the kind, and given the republican sympathies of the place it seems likely that some might regard "plans" for attaining national sovereignty in a more favorable light.

One such person is the man to whose report the narrator refers. John Wyse Power, a co-founder of the Gaelic Athletic Association with Michael Cusack, was both an ardent nationalist and, unlike Cusack, a devoted philosemite. His wife Jennie ran the food shop and restaurant in Henry Street where seven IRB members signed the Proclamation of Irish independence in April 1916—a shop that Nosey Flynn reports seeing Bloom come out of in Lestrygonians. These facts suggest that John Wyse Nolan may utter the words "it was Bloom gave the ideas for Sinn Fein to Griffith to put in his paper" in a spirit of respect rather than scorn.

Cyclops is not the only chapter that asserts a connection between Bloom and Griffith. In Penelope Molly thinks, "He was going about with some of them Sinner Fein lately or whatever they call themselves talking his usual trash and nonsense he says that little man he showed me without the neck is very intelligent the coming man Griffiths." This detail says something about the authorial design implicit in the motif, because Joyce admired Griffith, called the United Irishman the only worthwhile paper in Ireland, and found deep satisfaction in 1922 when the Free State came into being with Griffith as its leader.

The hugely destructive violence of the 1916 Rising, by contrast, only aggravated his despairing fear that Ireland might never escape from its historical nightmare. Evidently he wanted to associate his protagonist with a more hopeful course, and the fact that he does so in the Cyclops chapter makes perfect sense because it sets the pacifistic Bloom against a militant antagonist who advocates "force against force." Ironically, the Citizen bellows out "Sinn Fein! [...] Sinn Fein amhain! The friends we love are by our side and the foes we hate before us." But Griffith's nonviolent Sinn Féin plans give the lie to his use of the phrase.

If Bloom's Hungarian roots provide an obvious hook for grappling him to Griffith, his Jewishness would seem to disqualify him, given Griffith's dislike of Jews. But the reality here may be more complicated than it seems. Early drafts for Ulysses show that Joyce consulted the 12-volume Jewish Encyclopaedia (1901) as an authoritative source for Hebraic history and lore. Its chapter on Ireland's Jews suggests that a rabbi named Solomon Marcus Schiller-Szinessy brought ideas about the Hungarian revolution to Dublin.

Born in Budapest in 1820, Schiller-Szinessy was a close friend of the great statesman, orator, and revolutionary figure Lajos Kossuth, who became Hungary's leader in the 1848-49 war of independence. Schiller-Szinessy played a prominent role in the revolution by assembling and commanding a battalion of Jewish volunteers. Wounded in battle, captured, imprisoned, and condemned to death, he made a dramatic escape from a fortress and fled first to Trieste, then to Cork, and thence to Dublin, where he preached at the Mary's Abbey synagogue for a time before moving to England and gaining an appointment as lecturer in Talmudic Literature at Cambridge University.

After the war, Kossuth was feted and acclaimed in America, France, and Great Britain. This international acclaim may be sufficient to explain his mention in Circe. When Bloom is first proclaimed the Messiah, he "contracts his face so as to resemble many historical personages," among them "Kossuth." Schiller-Szinessy does not receive even such a brief mention in the novel, but his informing presence may be greater. Although he died in 1890 and left Dublin well before that, it seems entirely plausible that Leopold Bloom, raised by a devoutly Jewish Hungarian father, would have heard stories of this powerfully intellectual Hungarian rabbi who came to Dublin preaching a gospel of anti-imperial political autonomy. And Schiller-Szinessy would have been welcomed into the small company of prominent Dublin Jews who espoused anti-imperial politics, among them Lewis Wormser Harris, who was elected an alderman in 1874 (the first Jew to secure a place in the Corporation) and then Lord Mayor in 1876 (he died before he could take office). A man on whom Bloom may have been modeled, Albert Altman, followed in Harris's footsteps as a Jewish politician motivated by strong nationalist sentiments.

In 1903 Arthur Griffith endorsed Altman's candidacy as a councillor from the Usher's Quay ward. He also allied himself politically with Michael Noyk and Bethal Solomons, two other prominent Jews who espoused strongly nationalist views. Any one of these men might have given Joyce the idea of having a Jew advise Griffith. Altman family lore holds that the family started the Sinn Féin movement but that Dubliners have forgotten the fact. Solomons is mentioned in Finnegans Wake and his father Maurice in Ulysses. In James Joyce and the Politics of Egoism (2001), Jean-Michel Rabaté proposes that Noyk may have been the inspiration for John Wyse Nolan's report. There is no proof, but a wealth of circumstantial evidence suggests that Griffith may actually have been advised by one of Dublin's Jews.

Critical speculation about this possibility began with Hugh Kenner. While on a research trip to Dublin in the 1970s he stumbled across a rumour which suggested that Griffith employed, mirabile dictu, a "Jewish adviser ghost-writer" (Ulysses 133). As his letters to Adaline Glasheen show, Kenner was convinced that this rumour was of great significance, but despite his best endeavours he was unable to identify the man. In 1982, two years after the appearance of Kenner's book, Bernard Benstock reacted skeptically to the whole notion of Bloom as an intimate of Griffith: "It is not just that reason prevents us from accepting an historical movement founded by a fictional character, but that all the pieces in the puzzle conspire to show that no one is expected to believe this delightful absurdity. Two preferable sources are present to dispel any such silly idea: it is quite obvious from the thoughts on Griffith by both Leopold and Molly Bloom that our cautiously nonpolitical hero does not know Griffith well enough to advise him to tie his shoelace, much less found Sinn Fein" (On Reality in Ulysses). But the text of Ulysses seems to strongly suggest this.

In the years since this stark disagreement, only Rabaté has made a concerted effort to advance Kenner's hypothesis. Other critics have waffled between his credulity and Benstock's skepticism, trying not to be speared on the horns of a dilemma. In Joyce, Race and Empire (1995), Vincent Cheng tries to have it both ways, saying "it is quite unlikely that Bloom (even in fiction) was the man behind Arthur Griffith's ideas," but also wondering whether the linking of Bloom with Griffith "is a Joycean hint that there may be some truth" to the story. In Joyce and Nietszche (2013), Sam Slote threads the needle so subtly as to be almost unintelligible: "Since Bloom was a Jew of Hungarian descent, this implausible bit of gossip is lent enough credibility for some of his peers to believe it. And, in this way, the gossip about Griffith's Jewish advisor, which, while false, is based on a quantum of truth, mixes with the gossip about Bloom's religion to create a new falsehood that takes on a life of its own."

Two considerations probably underlie most of the skepticism: Griffith's antisemitism and Bloom's political irrelevance. Both could use some reevaluation. Studies like Brian Maye's Arthur Griffith (1997) are changing the popular impression of Griffith, suggesting that he was far from a hateful proto-fascist and that as time went on he steadily toned down his antisemitic rhetoric and acquired some Jewish friends. As for Bloom, Joyce jocoseriously intimates in Calypso, Wandering Rocks, and Eumaeus that there might be "a touch of the artist" in this unlettered man, a potential for writing a Ulysses-like "miniature cameo of the world we live in." If Bloom could have a bit of the novelist in him, then why not a bit of the leader who helped Ireland break out of the strangling embrace of English colonialism? The extravagant political fantasies in Circe show that Bloom's impulses to promote civic improvement go well beyond his plan of running a tramline "from the cattlemarket to the river."

John Hunt and Vincent Altman O'Connor 2026
